The what, why and how of thinking like a strategist, built on the seven-step problem-solving approach used by firms such as McKinsey.

Abd Karim Alias

November 2026

WHAT

Strategic thinking is a discipline, not a gift

It can be learned, practised and taught like any other leadership skill.

Strategic thinking is the disciplined ability to understand a complex situation, frame the real problem and choose a course of action that creates long-term advantage.

  • Zooms out to the whole system before zooming in
  • Starts from the question, not from the data
  • Makes explicit choices about what not to do
  • Turns analysis into a story people act on

STRATEGIC
THINKING

Big picture

Long horizon

Root causes

Hypotheses first

A clear story

Evidence over opinion

Choices and trade-offs

Systems and links

Strategic Thinking for Leaders

WHAT

Strategic thinking is not strategic planning

Planning works out how to get there. Thinking decides where there should be.

Strategic planning

Strategic thinking

Core question

How do we get there?

Where should we go, and why?

Mode

Analytical and sequential

Synthetic and exploratory

Rhythm

Annual cycle

Continuous

Output

Plans, budgets, KPIs

Insights, choices, options

Owner

Planning unit

Every leader

Planning without strategic thinking produces detailed maps to the wrong destination.

03

Strategic Thinking for Leaders

WHY

Six forces make it essential now

Yesterday's playbook is less reliable when these forces reinforce one another.

6

FORCES

01

Volatility

Shocks arrive faster, from pandemics to supply chains and geopolitics.

02

AI and automation

Routine analysis is cheap. Framing and judgement are scarce.

03

Information overload

More data than ever, but less clarity on what matters.

04

Shorter cycles

Advantages erode quickly as rivals copy and adapt.

05

Stakeholder scrutiny

Boards, regulators and the public expect defensible choices.

06

Connected problems

Talent, cost and climate no longer sit in one department.

SIX MUTUALLY REINFORCING FORCES

04

Strategic Thinking for Leaders

WHY

What goes wrong without it

The symptoms are visible. The thinking habits causing them sit below the waterline.

WHAT PEOPLE SEE

WHAT DRIVES IT

Firefighting the same crises every quarter

Initiatives launched, then quietly dropped

Treating symptoms

Fixing what is visible instead of the root cause.

Solution first

Jumping to an answer before the problem is clear.

Confirmation bias

Seeking only the evidence that agrees with us.

Data without a question

Commissioning reports that answer nothing in particular.

Silo thinking

Optimising one unit at the expense of the whole.

Hidden trade-offs

Saying yes to everything, so nothing gets real focus.

05

Strategic Thinking for Leaders

HOW

The seven-step problem-solving loop

Taught to new consultants at McKinsey and set out by Conn and McLean in Bulletproof Problem Solving (2019).

01

Define

Write a precise, decision-focused problem statement.

02

Disaggregate

Break the problem into a MECE issue tree.

03

Prioritise

Prune branches by impact and ability to act.

04

Plan the work

Assign analyses, owners and deadlines.

05

Analyse

Test hypotheses with the simplest robust evidence.

06

Synthesise

Find the so-what that answers the question.

07

Communicate

Lead with the answer, then the support.

FRAME

Steps 1 to 3

Get the question and its structure right

FIND

Steps 4 and 5

Gather just enough evidence to decide

TELL

Steps 6 and 7

Turn findings into a decision people act on

↻ Repeat the loop as new evidence arrives.

06

Strategic Thinking for Leaders

HOW · STEP 1

Define the problem before solving it

Running case. Sri Mutiara University has seen three years of falling new intake.

KEY QUESTION

How can Sri Mutiara University restore new undergraduate intake to 2,500 a year by September 2028 without lowering entry standards?

BOUNDARIES

CONTEXT

Intake has fallen three years running while rivals offer faster, cheaper pathways. A decision is due before the 2027 budget.

Decision-maker

Vice-Chancellor and Board, with Deans consulted

Success looks like

2,500 new students a year, fee income protected

Out of scope

New campuses and any change to entry standards

Illustrative case. Sri Mutiara University and all figures in this case are fictional.

“

A problem well stated is half solved.

Commonly attributed to Charles Kettering

A GOOD PROBLEM STATEMENT IS

Specific and measurable

Focused on a decision

Time-bound

Free of a built-in solution

07

Strategic Thinking for Leaders

HOW · STEP 2

Break it down with a MECE issue tree

Mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive. Every cause sits in one branch and nothing is missed.

KEY QUESTION

Why has new intake fallen 18% in three years?

Intake = applicants × offer rate × acceptance rate × registration rate

Fewer applicants

People are not applying

Smaller school-leaver pool

Lost share to competitors

Lower offer rate

We are not making offers

Stricter entry checks

Slow offer processing

Lower acceptance

Offers are being declined

Fees feel high for the value

Scholarships arrive too late

Fewer registering

Accepted students drop out

Financing falls through

Confusing onboarding

MECE CHECK

No overlap between branches

Branches multiply to the whole

Every leaf can be tested

LEADING HYPOTHESIS

Applications and offers are steady. The leak is in acceptance and registration.

08

Strategic Thinking for Leaders

HOW · STEP 3

Prioritise where to dig

Plot each branch by its likely impact and your ability to influence it.

SHAPE OVER TIME

ACT NOW

PARK

QUICK WINS

ABILITY TO INFLUENCE →

↑

IMPACT ON INTAKE

Fees vs value

Scholarship timing

Confusing onboarding

Slow offer processing

Smaller school-leaver pool

Lost share to competitors

Financing falls through

Stricter entry checks

THE 80/20 DISCIPLINE

  • Put most effort into the few branches that drive most of the answer
  • Drop branches you cannot influence and that move little
  • Write down what you chose not to study, and why

VERDICT FOR OUR CASE

Study fee value and scholarship timing first. Fix onboarding now as a quick win. Monitor demographics.

Day-one answer

State your best guess early, then actively try to disprove it.

10

Strategic Thinking for Leaders

HOW · STEPS 6 AND 7

Synthesise, then lead with the answer

Barbara Minto's Pyramid Principle, developed at McKinsey, puts the conclusion first and groups the support beneath it.

THE ANSWER

One governing thought

KEY ARGUMENTS

Three to five, MECE

SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

Data, analysis and examples

ILLUSTRATIVE STORYLINE

Restore intake by fixing conversion, not by chasing more applicants.

1

Declined offers cite value for money more than price alone

2

Scholarship letters arrive after most students have chosen

3

Accepted students fall away during a confusing onboarding

Open with situation, complication and question, then give the answer in the first minute.

11

Strategic Thinking for Leaders

APPLY

A portfolio lens with the BCG matrix

Bruce Henderson's growth-share matrix (BCG, 1970) helps leaders decide where to invest, hold or exit.

STARS

QUESTION MARKS

CASH COWS

DOGS

← High

Low →

RELATIVE MARKET SHARE

MARKET GROWTH →

Rendang ready meals

Plant-based snacks

Frozen roti

Sweet soy sauce

Canned curry

Illustrative case. Selera Nusantara Foods, a fictional Malaysian food manufacturer.

Stars

Invest to defend the lead

Question marks

Test fast, then commit or exit

Cash cows

Run efficiently, fund growth elsewhere

Dogs

Harvest, reposition or divest

THE STRATEGIC THINKING MOVE

Ask what the portfolio must look like in five years, then move money to match.

Treat the matrix as a conversation starter. It ignores synergies between units and can unfairly label teams.

12

Strategic Thinking for Leaders

APPLY

Balance today and tomorrow with Three Horizons

From McKinsey's The Alchemy of Growth (1999). Leaders manage three time horizons at once.

TIME →

↑ VALUE

H1

H2

H3

Many organisations use a rough 70/20/10 split of effort across core, adjacent and transformational bets. Treat it as a starting point, not a rule.

H1

Defend and extend the core

Lift conversion on existing degree programmes this intake cycle.

H2

Build emerging businesses

Stackable micro-credentials for working adults, scaled over two to three years.

H3

Create options for the future

Pilot AI-personalised learning pathways with regional industry partners.

13

Strategic Thinking for Leaders

APPLY

A 90-day roadmap to build the habit

Strategic thinking grows through deliberate practice on real problems, not through reading alone.

DAYS 1 TO 30

Frame

  • Write problem statements for your top three issues
  • Replace one status meeting with an issue-tree session

DAYS 31 TO 60

Practise

  • Run one full seven-step loop on a live problem
  • Send answer-first memos using the Pyramid Principle

DAYS 61 TO 90

Embed

  • Coach your team on MECE and prioritisation
  • Add a Three Horizons view to your next planning cycle

Day 0

Day 30

Day 60

Day 90

Lead with the answer

Tell people the conclusion first, then show why.
